shorts.title: El año empieza con una pregunta. (The year begins with a question)
shorts.description:
El año empieza con una pregunta. (The year begins with a question)

Not a resolution. Not a plan. Just one thing you genuinely want to know, about someone you already know well or someone you have only just met.

In Spanish there is a distinction that English flattens: preguntar means to ask a question, while pedir means to ask for something. The difference matters. A pregunta opens space. It does not demand anything back.

This year, what is one question you have not found the moment to ask yet?

shorts.title: You're surrounded by people and still not quite connecting.
shorts.description:
You're surrounded by people and still not quite connecting.

There is a specific kind of loneliness that has nothing to do with being alone. You are at a party, a dinner, a work drinks. You understand the words. You can follow the thread. And yet something stays just out of reach, the register is slightly off, the joke lands a second too late, and you smile at the right moment but you are not really in the room.

In Spanish there is a word for the small talk itself: cháchara. Light noise, not quite nothing but not quite something either. Most gatherings start there and many never leave.

What changes the room is a real question. Not an interrogation. Just something that asks a little more. That is what this episode of Mixed Signals is about.

Have you ever been in a room full of people and felt like the conversation never actually started? Tell us in the comments.

shorts.title: Anoche pasaron los Reyes. (Last night the Kings came by)
shorts.description:
Anoche pasaron los Reyes. (Last night the Kings came by)

On the night of 5 to 6 January, children in Spain leave their shoes by the door, sometimes with a little hay for the camels. In the morning the gifts are there. No chimney, no sleigh: three Kings arriving from the East, Melchor, Gaspar and Baltasar, whose names Spanish children know the way English children know Rudolph.

The day before, on the 5th, there is a cabalgata in most towns: a parade through the streets where the Kings throw sweets to the crowd. Adults line the pavement alongside children. It is not quite like anything in the British calendar.

If you are watching all of this for the first time from inside someone else's family, it can feel very beautiful and also very much theirs. The roscón de Reyes on the table, the specific excitement of the morning, the words said at the door when the shoes go out. Language is part of it. So is patience, and the willingness to ask what something means.

What is a tradition you have watched from the outside and grown to love? Tell us below.

shorts.title: El idioma de los nervios. (The language of nerves)
shorts.description:
El idioma de los nervios no siempre es el que hablas mejor. (The language of nerves is not always the one you speak best)

Meeting a partner's family for the first time is already one of the more loaded evenings in anyone's calendar. Add a language gap and something shifts. You cannot fall back on humour you know works. You cannot read the room as quickly. You smile a little more than usual, and hope it is landing right.

In Spanish the verb presentar covers introductions: te presento a mis padres, let me introduce you to my parents. It sounds formal in English. In Spanish it is simply what you say. But the moment itself, the handshake or the two kisses, the question you answer about where you are from, that is not covered by any verb.

What actually helps, beyond vocabulary, is knowing what the evening is for. In a Spanish family context, the first dinner is often long. Sobremesa happens. There will be pauses that do not feel awkward to anyone else at the table. Sitting inside that rhythm, rather than trying to fill it, can be its own kind of belonging.

If this has been your experience, we would like to hear it in the comments.

shorts.title: Which language do the conversations that really matter happen in?
shorts.description:
Which language do the conversations that really matter happen in?

Researchers who study bilingualism have noticed the same thing for decades. When something is high-stakes, frightening or deeply personal, people tend to reach for the language they grew up in. Not because the other language is not good enough, but because the first language carries a different kind of weight.

There is a Spanish term that sits close to this: de corazón, from the heart. And the question of which language your heart works in is not a small one. Couples who do not share a first language describe it as one of the quietest tensions in a relationship: not an argument, just a room you cannot quite enter.

We would like to know what you think.

Which language do you turn to when the conversation is important?

shorts.title: You are at the table and everyone shares a language you are still learning.
shorts.description:
You are at the table and everyone shares a language you are still learning.

There is a specific kind of quiet that happens in that moment. Not unfriendly, not unkind. Just fast. And you are half a beat behind every sentence.

Linguists sometimes call it anxiety in the second language, though that phrase does not quite capture it. It is more physical than that: a tightness, a slight heat, the feeling of reaching for a word and finding air. In Spanish you might say me quedé en blanco, I went blank, which is exactly right.

The moments that shift it are rarely big. Someone slows down. Someone asks you something directly. Someone laughs at something you said, with you, not past you.

That is what this episode of Mixed Signals is about.

shorts.title: Tranquilo. (It's fine, no rush)
shorts.description:
Tranquilo. (It's fine, no rush)

Some words don't need translating. Tranquilo is one of them. It sits somewhere between calm down, it's fine and no rush, and it only sounds right when you hear it in context, said at exactly the right moment across a café table.

In January in Spain the bars are quieter than they were in December. The rush of las Navidades has passed. People come back to their regular seats, their regular order, their regular hour. The pace drops, and tranquilo is one of the first words to return.

Language learners often say that understanding the rhythm of a place comes before the vocabulary. The sounds teach you how the day moves: when voices lower, when chairs scrape back, when nothing needs to be said at all.

What's one word or sound from another language that feels like a whole atmosphere to you? Tell us in the comments.

shorts.title: ¿Qué te trajo aquí? (What brought you here?)
shorts.description:
¿De dónde eres? Es casi siempre la pregunta equivocada. (Where are you from? It's almost always the wrong question)

In January people host more than they admit. Someone visits from somewhere else. Someone brings a partner home for the first time. And the first question that surfaces, almost automatically, is de dónde eres.

It is not a bad question. But it is a thin one. It hands the answer back to the other person as a label, and labels tend to close conversations rather than open them. Researchers who study intercultural communication have noted for years that origin questions put the responder in a position of explaining themselves rather than sharing themselves. That is a different thing.

The better questions are slower. ¿Qué es lo que más echas de menos de donde creciste? What do you miss most about where you grew up? Or simply: ¿Qué te trajo aquí? What brought you here? One word changes the whole room.

We'd love to know: what's the best question someone ever asked you when you arrived somewhere new?

The Journal has more on this:

https://profluency.co.uk/journal/the-question-that-turned-dinner-into-a-conversation/

shorts.title: Where are you from? It depends who's asking.
shorts.description:
Where are you from? It depends who's asking.

Mixed Signals is about the moments when language and expectation don't quite line up.

De dónde eres is one of the most common questions in any language. In Spanish it is light, sociable, an opener. But the same question can land very differently depending on who asks it, what accent they heard first and what they expected the answer to be. Researchers in sociolinguistics call this the loaded question problem: the words are neutral but the context is not.

If you grew up between two languages or two countries, you've probably learned to give the short answer because the long one takes too much explanation. And the short answer is almost never the whole truth.

What do you say when someone asks you that question? And what do you wish they'd asked instead? Let us know in the comments.

shorts.title: Enero tiene su propia quietud. (January has its own quietness)
shorts.description:
Enero tiene su propia quietud. (January has its own quietness)

After Reyes, something settles in Spain. The decorations come down slowly, the streets go quiet, and January finds its own rhythm. It is not quite melancholy. It is closer to the feeling of a room after everyone has gone home.

There is a Spanish word that sits at the centre of that feeling: madrugada. It means the hours between midnight and dawn, but it carries more than a time. It holds the particular quality of being awake when the city is not, the stillness before the day makes its demands. English reaches for "the small hours" or "the early morning" and both fall a little short.

Language researchers call these lexical gaps, words one language needs and another has never bothered to build. They are not accidents. They point to the things a culture decided were worth naming.

What is the January word in your language?

shorts.description:
¿Qué pregunta te arrepientes de no haber hecho? (What do you regret never asking?)

Some questions sit with you for years. Not because they were difficult to answer, but because you never got around to asking them. The evening was full, the moment passed, and now the person is in another city or another chapter of their life.

That is what a good conversation question actually does. It does not break the ice. It makes time for the thing you wanted to know but were waiting for permission to say.

shorts.title: Madrugada. (The hours between midnight and dawn)
shorts.description:
Madrugada. (The hours between midnight and dawn)

In Spain the word madrugada does not just mean early morning. It names the hours that belong to nobody in particular: after the last people have gone home and before the first ones arrive somewhere new. The city is there but it is not quite itself.

English reaches for "the small hours" or "the early hours" and both are accurate and both fall slightly short. Madrugada holds the texture of that time, not just its position on a clock.

If you have ever been awake at that hour in a city where you do not speak the language, you will know that it has its own particular feeling. Quieter than you expected. More yours than you expected.
